title: Fetch API
summary: The **Fetch API** is the modern, promise-based way to make HTTP requests from the browser. `fetch(url)` returns a promise that resolves to a `Response` object — and importantly, it only rejects on network failure, not on HTTP error statuses like 404 or 500.

subtopics.title: fetch returns a promise for a Response
subtopics.explanation: Calling `fetch(url)` starts the request and immediately returns a promise. That promise resolves to a `Response` object representing the HTTP response — its status, headers, and a body stream — not the parsed data yet. You then read the body with a method like `.json()` or `.text()`.
subtopics.example:
const res = await fetch('/api/users');
console.log(res.status); // e.g. 200

subtopics.title: Reading the body with response.json()
subtopics.explanation: The Response body is a stream that you must read and parse. `response.json()` reads the stream to completion and returns a promise that resolves to the parsed JavaScript value. Because it returns a promise, you await it (or chain a second .then). You can only read the body once.
subtopics.example:
const res = await fetch(url);
const data = await res.json();

subtopics.title: fetch does NOT reject on 4xx/5xx
subtopics.explanation: A common surprise: fetch's promise only rejects on network-level failures (offline, DNS, CORS). An HTTP 404 or 500 still resolves successfully. You must check `response.ok` (true for 200–299) or `response.status` yourself and throw if the request failed.

subtopics.title: Headers, methods, and request body
subtopics.explanation: Pass a second options argument to configure the request: `method` (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE), `headers` (e.g. Content-Type), and `body` (often a JSON string). For JSON bodies you stringify the data and set the Content-Type header so the server parses it correctly.

subtopics.title: Using fetch with async/await
subtopics.explanation: fetch pairs naturally with async/await: await the fetch to get the Response, check ok, then await the body parser. This reads top-to-bottom and lets you wrap the whole flow in try/catch for both network and HTTP errors.
subtopics.example: async function getUsers(){ const r = await fetch('/api/users'); if(!r.ok) throw new Error('failed'); return r.json(); }

subtopics.title: Error handling
subtopics.explanation: Robust fetch code distinguishes two failure types: network errors (the promise rejects, caught by try/catch) and HTTP errors (the promise resolves but response.ok is false). Handle both — check ok and throw, and wrap the call in try/catch — so neither silently slips through.
subtopics.example: try { const r = await fetch(url); if(!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status); } catch(e){ /* network or HTTP */ }

subtopics.title: Cancelling with AbortController (note)
subtopics.explanation: To cancel an in-flight request (e.g. a user navigates away or types a new search), create an AbortController, pass its `signal` to fetch, and call `controller.abort()` to cancel. The fetch promise then rejects with an AbortError you can detect and ignore.

subtopics.title: CORS basics
subtopics.explanation: Browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy: requests to a different origin (scheme+host+port) are restricted unless the server opts in with CORS headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin. CORS is controlled by the server, not the client — fetch can't bypass it; a missing header causes the request to fail with a CORS error.

foundations.overview: The Fetch API is the browser's built-in interface for making HTTP requests. `fetch(url, options)` returns a promise that resolves to a Response object; you then read its body (JSON, text, blob) which is itself async. It replaces the older XMLHttpRequest with a cleaner, promise-based design that works seamlessly with async/await.
foundations.formalDefinition: fetch() is a global function that initiates a network request and returns a Promise<Response>. The Response exposes status, headers, and body-reading methods (json, text, blob, etc.), each returning a promise. The fetch promise rejects only on network-level errors, not on unsuccessful HTTP statuses.
foundations.whyItMatters: Communicating with servers is the core of nearly every web app — loading data, submitting forms, calling APIs. fetch is the standard, dependency-free way to do it, and its quirks (no rejection on 4xx/5xx) are a frequent source of real bugs and interview questions.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of fetch in two steps: first you get the envelope (the Response — was it delivered? what status?), then you open it to read the letter inside (the body, via .json()). Delivery succeeding doesn't mean the letter says yes.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser performs the request on a background network thread and resolves the fetch promise's continuation as a microtask once headers arrive. Body reading streams the response and resolves when fully read. CORS checks happen in the browser before exposing the response.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Loading API data into components, submitting forms with POST, polling endpoints, uploading files, cancelling stale search requests with AbortController, and calling third-party APIs all use fetch.
foundations.businessImpact: Reliable fetch code with proper error handling means fewer broken screens, clearer error messages, and graceful behavior when APIs fail — directly affecting user trust and conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing fetch's contract (Response vs. data, ok-checking, two-failure-types) prevents a class of bugs where 404/500 responses are treated as success and crash downstream code.
foundations.performanceImpact: fetch is non-blocking; performance issues come from not parallelizing independent requests, not cancelling stale ones (wasting bandwidth), or fetching too eagerly. AbortController and caching mitigate this.
commonUseCases: GET requests to load and render API data
POST/PUT requests with a JSON body to create or update resources
Cancelling outdated requests (type-ahead search) with AbortController
Centralized error handling that checks response.ok and parses JSON

commonMisconceptions.myth: fetch rejects its promise when the server returns 404 or 500.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It resolves successfully on any HTTP response; you must check response.ok or response.status and throw yourself.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The fetch promise resolves to the parsed data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It resolves to a Response object; you must call .json()/.text() (also async) to get the actual data.

debuggingLab.title: Treating a 404 as success
debuggingLab.symptom: When the API returns 404, the code crashes with 'Cannot read properties of undefined' instead of showing an error.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: fetch resolves even for a 404, so the code proceeds to parse the body. The error response has no `name` field, so `user.name` is undefined and calling `.toUpperCase()` throws. The missing step is checking `response.ok`.
commonMistakes: Assuming fetch rejects on HTTP error statuses like 404 or 500.
Skipping the response.ok check and parsing the body unconditionally.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Check the response status before parsing so a 404 produces a clear error instead of a crash.

theory.question: What does fetch return, and how do you get the actual data from it?
theory.directAnswer: fetch returns a promise that resolves to a Response object — not the data. The Response describes the HTTP result (status, headers, ok). To get the data you call a body method like response.json() (or .text()), which is also async, so you await it too.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: fetch is a Promise<Response> API; the Response wraps status/headers and a one-time-readable body stream.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A two-step design (response, then body) lets you inspect status/headers before deciding how to read the body, and supports streaming large responses.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The first await resolves once headers arrive; the body method reads and parses the stream and resolves with the value.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing Response with data is a top beginner mistake; interviewers check that you know the two-step, two-await pattern.
theory.realWorldExample: const res = await fetch('/api/cart'); const cart = await res.json();

nestedTopics.title: Response object
nestedTopics.explanation: Holds status, ok, headers, and body-reading methods.

nestedTopics.title: Body methods
nestedTopics.explanation: json(), text(), blob() each return a promise and can run only once.

nestedTopics.title: Two awaits
nestedTopics.explanation: One for the response, one for parsing the body.

followUps.question: Why can you read the body only once?
followUps.answer: The body is a stream; reading consumes it. Call response.clone() first if you need to read it twice.

theory.question: Why doesn't fetch reject on HTTP errors like 404 or 500, and how should you handle them?
theory.directAnswer: fetch only rejects on network-level failures (offline, DNS, CORS). Any HTTP response — including 404 and 500 — is considered a successful round trip, so the promise resolves. You must inspect response.ok (true for 200–299) or response.status and throw an error yourself when the status indicates failure.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A deliberate contract: 'the request reached the server and came back' is success, regardless of status code.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An error status is a valid, informative response (with a body and headers), not a transport failure, so fetch surfaces it instead of throwing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Check res.ok and throw; wrap the whole call in try/catch so both HTTP and network failures are handled in one place.

theory.whyImportant: It causes a very common bug where error responses are parsed as success and crash downstream code; interviewers test awareness of it.
theory.realWorldExample: if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status) before res.json().

nestedTopics.title: response.ok
nestedTopics.explanation: Boolean true when status is in the 200–299 range.

nestedTopics.title: Two failure types
nestedTopics.explanation: Network rejection vs. HTTP error you detect via ok.

followUps.question: How is this different from axios?
followUps.answer: axios rejects automatically on non-2xx statuses, so you don't need the ok-check, though you still catch the rejection.

scenario.question: In a type-ahead search box, fast typing causes results to flicker and sometimes an old query's results overwrite the newest. How do you fix it with fetch?
scenario.directAnswer: This is a race condition between in-flight requests. I'd use AbortController: before starting a new request, abort the previous one by calling controller.abort(), and pass the controller's signal to fetch. The stale request rejects with an AbortError I ignore, so only the latest query's results render.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A request race where slower earlier responses arrive after newer ones and clobber the UI.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Each keystroke fires an independent fetch; responses can return out of order.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: AbortController.signal lets you cancel the prior fetch; aborting makes its promise reject with AbortError, which you detect and skip.

scenario.whyImportant: Request races are a classic real-world frontend bug and a strong signal of practical fetch knowledge.

nestedTopics.title: AbortController
nestedTopics.explanation: Creates a signal you pass to fetch and an abort() to cancel it.

nestedTopics.title: AbortError
nestedTopics.explanation: The rejection thrown when a request is cancelled; ignore it intentionally.

followUps.question: Besides aborting, how else can you guard against stale results?
followUps.answer: Track the latest request id/timestamp and ignore responses that don't match the current query, or debounce input to fire fewer requests.

coding.question: Implement fetchWithTimeout(url, ms) that rejects if the request takes longer than `ms` milliseconds, using AbortController.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll create an AbortController, start a timer that calls controller.abort() after `ms`, and pass the signal to fetch. On success I clear the timer and return the response; if aborted, fetch rejects with AbortError, which I can surface as a timeout error.
coding.lineByLine: We create a controller and schedule abort() after `ms`. fetch receives the signal so it can be cancelled. On success we return the response. If the abort fired, fetch rejects with an AbortError we convert to a clear timeout error; other errors rethrow. finally clears the timer so it never fires late.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) overhead beyond the network request.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — a controller and a timer reference.

alternativeApproaches.title: Promise.race with a timeout promise
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Race the fetch against a setTimeout-rejecting promise, but this doesn't actually cancel the request like AbortController does.

followUps.question: Why is AbortController better than Promise.race for timeouts?
followUps.answer: AbortController truly cancels the underlying request, freeing the connection; Promise.race only stops waiting while the request keeps running in the background.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Production apps wrap fetch in a small client module that centralizes base URLs, default headers (auth tokens), ok-checking, JSON parsing, and error normalization, so feature code calls high-level functions like api.getUsers().
productionDeepDive.performance: Parallelize independent requests, cancel stale ones with AbortController, add caching/conditional requests (ETag), and debounce request-triggering input to cut redundant network traffic.
productionDeepDive.security: Respect CORS (server-controlled), send credentials only when needed, never put secrets in client code, validate and sanitize responses, and use HTTPS. Be deliberate about the `credentials` option for cookies.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Bound concurrency for bulk requests, implement retries with backoff for transient failures, and handle rate limits (429) gracefully rather than retrying instantly.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: A single fetch wrapper avoids scattering ok-checks and headers everywhere; consistent error shapes make UI error handling uniform and testable.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log request URLs, statuses, and latencies; capture failed fetches and AbortErrors separately so monitoring distinguishes real failures from intentional cancellations.

caseStudies.problem: Scattered fetch calls duplicated error handling and missed ok-checks.
caseStudies.solution: Introduced a centralized fetch client with ok-checking, JSON parsing, and auth headers.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Adds a thin abstraction layer to maintain.
caseStudies.lessons: Centralizing fetch logic eliminates a whole class of inconsistent-error bugs.

keyTakeaways: fetch returns a promise that resolves to a Response object — call .json()/.text() (also async) to get the data.
fetch only rejects on network failures; HTTP errors like 404/500 still resolve, so always check response.ok.
Configure requests with the options object: method, headers, and a (usually stringified JSON) body.
Use AbortController to cancel in-flight requests and avoid stale results or wasted bandwidth.
CORS is enforced by the browser and controlled by the server — the client cannot bypass it.
